messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: trapping exceptions in R
parts:
I think we only need a try/catch arrangement to
catch the index out of bounds errors. Unlike the
domain errors, they don't get trapped and treated
as zero probability by the sampler.

Daniel or I can help if you (Jiqiang) need some
help with try/catch.

I believe the index exceptions are the only ones
we throw, but we should check.

- Bob

On 9/1/12 5:13 PM, Michael Braun wrote:
> Fixed the problem. Once I exported the data, and ran stan from a shell, I got the following helpful message:
>
> Exception: INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=5; lower bound=1; upper bound=4; index position=1; xi
>
> Diagnostic information:
> Dynamic exception type: std::out_of_range
> std::exception::what: INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=5; lower bound=1; upper bound=4; index position=1; xi
>
> This told me that I was interpreting the statement
>
> vector[N] xi[k]
>
> incorrectly. I thought it meant a vector of N k-dimensional arrays, when in fact it is a vector of k N-dimensional
> arrays. Once I fixed that, it all worked.
>
> It might be useful for those messages to pass through the rstan package somehow.

On Sun, Sep 2, 2012 at 6:14 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
I think we only need a try/catch arrangement to
catch the index out of bounds errors.  Unlike the
domain errors, they don't get trapped and treated
as zero probability by the sampler.

Daniel or I can help if you (Jiqiang) need some
help with try/catch.

Well, I have the try/catch to catch all exceptions and pass the error message to R. It is like

try {

} catch (std::exception& e) {
  // pass the error to R
} catch (...)  {
  // print the error message in R 
}

So I do not think I can do better, but I hope I understood wrongly so we can prevent R from crashing sometimes.  Ben thinks the message is passed to R, but R crashes before that.

I believe the index exceptions are the only ones
we throw, but we should check.

- Bob

On 9/1/12 5:13 PM, Michael Braun wrote:
Fixed the problem.  Once I exported the data, and ran stan from a shell, I got the following helpful message:

Exception: INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=5; lower bound=1; upper bound=4; index position=1; xi

Diagnostic information:
Dynamic exception type: std::out_of_range
std::exception::what: INDEX OPERATOR [] OUT OF BOUNDS; index=5; lower bound=1; upper bound=4; index position=1; xi

This told me that I was interpreting the statement

  vector[N] xi[k]

incorrectly.  I thought it meant a vector of N k-dimensional arrays, when in fact it is a vector of k N-dimensional
arrays. Once I fixed that, it all worked.

It might be useful for those messages to pass through the rstan package somehow.
--

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] trapping exceptions in R
parts:
My understanding is that the out-of-range error on a std::vector triggered a SIGABRT. According to

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIGABRT

you can catch those. But I think the best can be done at that point is to call exit().

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: NDEBUG, STAN_NO_DEBUG and array, etc. index validation
parts:
Two things.

First, we should be turning off Eigen validation in
Stan in the makefiles using the -DEIGEN_NO_DEBUG option to
set the EIGEN_NO_DEBUG property.

We're already checking those ranges ourselves.

On 9/3/12 8:04 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> That sounds like a good idea, as long as it can be turned off with -DNDEBUG or whatever. I don't know how to do that for
> std::vectors though.

Second, we just need to go through the getters
(I think in math/matrix) and apply the relevant
#ifdefs.

I think I've been putting it off because I'm
really opposed to preprocessor voodoo. But this
I can live with.

Just to confirm, I think the decision was to turn
off Stan range checking if either the NDEBUG or STAN_NO_DEBUG
property was defined (e.g., by using -DSTAN_NO_DEBUG as a compiler
argument).

I'll push that through unless anyone objects.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] NDEBUG, STAN_NO_DEBUG and array, etc. index validation
parts:
That seems reasonable. Eigen uses EIGEN_NO_DEBUG everywhere in its
own source and then defines that when NDEBUG is defined to allow
selective debugging. (I.E., you can turn on EIGEN_NO_DEBUG without
turning on NDEBUG for everything.)

Cheers,
Marcus
